notes.label: Praeteritio
notes.body: Nepos says he will pass over Philip (Philip V, king of Macedon, who allied with Hannibal against Rome in 215 BC) yet names him all the same. This lets him slip in one more example of Hannibal turning a king against Rome without breaking off from the story of Antiochus, so the reader sees Antiochus as part of a pattern.

notes.label: Emphatic placement of absens
notes.body: absens comes straight after quem, ahead of the rest of the clause, so the stress falls on the fact that Hannibal made Philip Rome's enemy without being there in person. This shows how far his hatred could reach, since even at a distance his influence was enough to turn a king against Rome.

notes.label: Superlative
notes.body: Calling Antiochus (Antiochus III, ruler of the Seleucid empire, to whom Hannibal fled in 195 BC) the most powerful king of the age raises his status as high as it can go. The greater the king, the more impressive it is that Hannibal could steer him against Rome.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.quote: omnium iis temporibus potentissimus rex Antiochus
notes.body: omnium is separated from potentissimus by iis temporibus and placed first in the sentence. Opening with "of all" stresses the scale of Antiochus's power before we know who is meant, and his name is saved for the end as the climax.

notes.label: Fire metaphor
notes.body: incendit means "set on fire", so Hannibal is presented as the spark that ignites Antiochus's desire for war. Fire suits the idea because it spreads quickly and is hard to control, which suggests that once Hannibal has lit it, the king's eagerness grows far beyond where it started (as the Red Sea clause then shows). It also makes Hannibal the active force and Antiochus the one acted upon, so the drive for war against Rome clearly comes from Hannibal.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: bellandi ("of waging war") belongs with cupiditate but is held back until after the verb. This puts "war" in the final position of the clause, so it lands with extra weight and leaves no doubt about what Hannibal's influence was directed towards.

notes.label: Geographical extremes
notes.body: Nepos marks the two ends of the planned expedition, from the Red Sea at the eastern edge of Antiochus's empire all the way to Italy. Stretching the war across almost the whole known world shows how vast an undertaking Hannibal inspired, and so how powerful his hatred of Rome must be to have set it in motion.

notes.label: Final position of Italiae
notes.body: Italiae is the last word of the sentence, so the target of the whole enterprise is held back until the end. The delay builds towards Rome's homeland as the climax, making Italy feel like the destination of everything Hannibal has stirred up.

notes.label: Periodic sentence
notes.quote: ad quem cum legati venissent ... tempore dato adiit ad regem
notes.body: The sentence piles up clauses about the Roman envoys and their plot (cum ... venissent, qui ... explorarent darentque, ut ... adducerent, tamquam ... sentiret) and then Hannibal's discovery of it, and the main verb adiit only arrives at the very end. The reader is kept waiting and hemmed in, much as Hannibal is hemmed in by the scheme, so that when the main verb finally comes it shows him breaking out and acting decisively.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The repeated hard c binds "plans" and "secret" together so that they are heard as a single idea, plotting done out of sight. By making the secrecy stand out, Nepos presents the Roman envoys as sly and underhand, which colours how the reader judges Rome in this episode.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: The Romans work through secret plans, whereas Hannibal responds by openly reminding the king of his loyalty (fide). Setting Roman deceit against Hannibal's frankness makes him the more trustworthy figure, and makes his hatred of Rome seem more understandable given how the Romans behave.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: The envoys aim to make Antiochus think Hannibal has been bribed (corruptus) by the Romans themselves (ab ipsis). The irony is that the only ones acting corruptly are the Romans, who are secretly deceiving the king, while the man they accuse of being bought is the one whose hatred of Rome could never be bought. ipsis sharpens this, since the accusation comes from the very people guilty of underhand dealing.

notes.label: Alliteration (minor point)
notes.body: The repeated a sound ties together "different" and "before", underlining the change of heart the Romans want Antiochus to believe in. The sound draws attention to the very lie being spread, that Hannibal is no longer the man he was.

notes.label: Polysyndeton
notes.quote: neque id frustra fecissent idque Hannibal comperisset seque ... segregari vidisset
notes.body: Three clauses are joined by repeated connectives: neque ("and ... not"), idque ("and this") and seque ("and himself"). Each connective adds a new stage (the plot works, Hannibal finds out, he sees himself shut out), and chaining them together makes the stages pile up one after another. The pressure on Hannibal builds quickly, so the reader feels his position worsening just before he acts.

notes.label: Vivid word choice
notes.body: segregari comes from se + grex and literally means "to be separated from the flock", while interioribus consiliis pictures an inner circle of advisers. Together they show Hannibal being cut off and left outside, and the passive voice stresses that this is being done to him, which makes his danger clear and explains why he must speak up.

notes.label: Pairing of key ideas
notes.quote: de fide sua et odio in Romanos
notes.body: Loyalty (fide) and hatred of Rome (odio in Romanos) are placed side by side as the two things Hannibal stresses. Linking them shows that for Hannibal they go together, since his hatred of Rome is the proof of his loyalty to Antiochus, which is exactly the argument the anecdote that follows is designed to support.

notes.label: Direct speech
notes.body: Nepos switches from reporting what Hannibal said to giving his own words. This makes the moment more vivid and dramatic, and because the story comes from Hannibal's own mouth it carries his personal authority, so the hatred is something he himself declares.

notes.label: Emphatic word order
notes.body: pater meus opens the speech, ahead even of Hamilcar's name. Putting "my father" first frames everything that follows as an inheritance, so the hatred is presented as a family duty handed down from father to son.

notes.label: Diminutive
notes.body: puerulus is a diminutive of puer, meaning "little boy". It stresses how young Hannibal was, which shows how deeply rooted his hatred is, since it was instilled before he was old enough to choose it and has shaped his whole life since.

notes.label: Precise detail of age
notes.quote: utpote non amplius VIIII annos nato
notes.body: Giving an exact age adds a specific, memorable detail that makes the story sound authentic. It also reinforces the diminutive, and non amplius ("no more than") even hints that he may have been younger, emphasising how early the hatred began.

notes.label: Solemn religious formula
notes.body: "Best and greatest" is the formal cult title of Jupiter used in official worship. Such grand, ceremonial language raises the tone and makes the scene feel sacred, so the hatred that comes out of it seems sanctioned by the gods and therefore binding.

notes.label: Ritual setting
notes.body: The sacrifice of victims creates a formal religious occasion, which prepares for the oath that follows. An oath sworn in such a setting is all the more serious, so the scene builds up the weight of the promise Hannibal is about to describe.

notes.label: Roman name for a Carthaginian god
notes.body: The god Hamilcar sacrificed to was Carthaginian (probably Baal Hammon), but Nepos gives him Jupiter's name. This makes the scene familiar to a Roman reader, who would immediately grasp how solemn and binding a sacrifice to the chief god was.
